holidays.name: The Ides of March
holidays.description: Beware! This is the day Julius Caesar was famously warned about. Fans of history, drama and dramatic irony mark it with Roman-themed feasts, toga-clad gatherings, and plenty of jokes about watching your back. Some people stab at a Caesar salad in tribute.
holidays.origin: In the Roman calendar, the Ides fell around the middle of the month, on the 15th in March. The day became infamous in 44 BCE, when Julius Caesar was assassinated in Rome by a group of senators. Shakespeare later immortalized the warning to beware this date.
holidays.funFact: The Ides were not originally ominous. In Rome, the Ides of March was a festival day honoring the god Mars, and it was also a deadline for settling debts.

holidays.name: National Peanut Lovers Day
holidays.description: A salute to the humble legume that is not actually a nut. Celebrate with peanut butter sandwiches, brittle, satay, or a handful of roasted peanuts straight from the shell.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin, and it fits right in during National Peanut Month in March.
holidays.funFact: Peanuts grow underground, not on trees. They are legumes, closer to peas and lentils than to almonds or walnuts.

holidays.name: World Consumer Rights Day
holidays.description: A global day for shoppers everywhere to stand up for fair prices, safe products, honest advertising, and the right to be heard. It is a good excuse to read the fine print and ask for a refund.
holidays.origin: The day marks a 1962 address to the U.S. Congress by President John F. Kennedy, who outlined basic consumer rights. Consumer groups around the world began observing it in 1983 and now organize yearly campaigns around it.
holidays.funFact: Kennedy's 1962 speech was among the first times a head of state formally laid out consumer rights, including safety, information, choice, and the right to be heard.
